en: Then, according to the prescribed procedure for the *gaṇacakra*, having satisfied those who have entered the maṇḍala hall with food, drink, and other offerings dedicated to the circle, and having honored them together through a night vigil with dance, song, and so forth, as well as the practice of *bodhicitta*, he says: "The maṇḍala must not be shown to anyone, nor should you speak of what has occurred here. Having said this, he dismisses the disciples. Then, having performed the offerings of the *digbali* and other rites outside, he enters within, bows to the circle, and presents the *argha* and other offerings to the Lord of the Circle (*cakreśa*).
Having dedicated the merit, circumambulated the maṇḍala three times clockwise, and stood at the eastern gate facing the Blessed One, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra three times.

Having spoken thus, through the ritual of the gaṇacakra, one should offer food, drink, and so forth to the maṇḍala within the maṇḍala hall, and thereby bring those who have entered it to complete satisfaction.

Together with them, one should offer authentic worship through dance, song, and so forth, as well as through reflections on the bodhicitta, without sleeping during the night; then one should say: "You must not speak of this entrance to anyone."

Then, having dismissed the disciples and performed the external offerings, *bali* rites, and so forth, he enters within, prostrates to the wheel, and presents the water for the feet (*argha*) and other offerings to the lord of the wheel. Having fully dedicated the merits, he circumambulates the mandala three times to the right.
Facing the Blessed One, he stands at the eastern gate and recites the hundred-syllable mantra three times.

Having requested forbearance with the words beginning "And by non-attainment," and having performed the dedication with the words beginning "The welfare of all sentient beings has been accomplished for you," one should dismiss the wisdom-circle (*jñānacakra*) with *oṃ āḥ hūṃ vajra mur*, internalize the self-manifested maṇḍala within oneself, and recite: *oṃ akāro mukhaṃ sarvadharmāṇām ādyanutpannatvāt oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Uttering "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Mur" and resolving upon the non-arising of all phenomena while ringing the bell, one should erase [the lines] starting from the eastern gate along the path of the Brahma-thread up to the location of the central deity, using the vajra held in the hand; having placed a mere speck of powder on one's own head, one should erase the lotus and so forth.

With the words beginning with "I have not obtained," and so forth, one requests forbearance; then, with the words beginning with "You have accomplished all the aims of sentient beings," and by reciting *oṃ āḥ hūṃ vajra muḥ*, one requests the departure of the wisdom maṇḍala, and dissolves one's own emanated maṇḍala into oneself.

Reciting "oṃ āḥ hūṃ muḥ" and with the conviction that all phenomena are unarisen, ring the bell and, holding the vajra in one's hand, starting from the eastern gate, mark the path of the Brahma-lines up to the central location; then, sprinkling a little colored powder on the head, one should clear away the lotuses and so forth.
Then, one should carve out the doors and the corners with lines of the vajra held in the hand.
Then, the doors and the corners should also be delineated with the tip of the vajra held in the hand.

Thereafter, with the four *hūṃ*s: "Oṃ, Vajrakīla, uproot all stakes by the command of Vajradhara! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ hor! one should extract the stakes using the *pratyālīḍha* posture and the *saṃdaṃśa* (tongs) mudrā. Then, one should bathe them with milk over which the mantra "Oṃ ruru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddha locane sarvārthasādhani svāhā" has been recited one hundred and eight times.

Following that, with the mantra *oṃ vajrakīla utkīlaya sarvakīlan vajradhara ājñāya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ hoḥ*, one should extract the kīlas using the four *hūṃ*s and the mudrā of the left leg extended and the right knee drawn up. Then, they should be washed with milk over which the mantra *oṃ ru ru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddhi locane sarvārthasādhane svāhā* has been recited one hundred and eight times.
One should dismiss the deities of the *kīla* and fill the pits of the *kīla*. For those seeking pacification and other benefits, one should give a small amount of colored powder (*rajas*) to each.
One should request the deities of the *kīla* to depart and fill the holes of the *kīla*. To those who desire pacification and so forth, a little of the colored powder should be given.
Thus, having made the mandala house secluded, one should remove the dust; afterwards, the skillful practitioner should sprinkle the entire circle with cow’s milk alone.
Thereafter, he performs the smearing with cow dung, as well as the anointing and drawing of the lines.
Having performed a prostration by scattering flowers, one should satisfy the Earth.

Likewise, having cleared the maṇḍala house of people, the colored powders should be properly gathered. Afterwards, those born of cow-products should skillfully scatter [the remains] all around the wheel. Then, an anointing with cow-products should be performed, and the lines should also be anointed.
Having scattered flowers and performed prostrations, one should please the Earth Goddess.

Afterwards, having filled the *śrīvijaya* with colored powder (*rajas*), one should likewise prepare the jar for Vighnāri with ashes and other materials according to the ritual rule, these two having fine cloths around their necks (*kaṇṭha*).
Then, upon a *dhṛtasidhra* held by a *yoginī*, and likewise during the festival of the *caryāṇaka*:
Having led [the victim] there and performed the *nāgabali* offering, one should cast everything into a river or a lake.

Subsequently, the glorious Vijayā fills [the vessel] with colored powders (*rajas*) and likewise places the ashes of the sacrificial fire and so forth into the *vighnāntaka* vase. With these supreme ritual garments around her neck, she is taken up by the Yoginī and carried high upon the back of an elephant; then, the *nāga* bali is offered.
Having performed [the ritual], one should pour [the water] into rivers or lakes.

According to this procedure, having led the Ācārya or the disciple—seated upon a palanquin or similar vehicle on an elephant or other mount, adorned with garments provided by the patron (dānapati)—to a great river, a large lake, or deep water, one should sit on the bank on ground smeared with cow dung. Having drawn a maṇḍala with white perfumes and painted an eight-petaled lotus in its center, one should place Vajrasattva in the pericarp and the eight Nāgas upon the petals.

Having worshipped as before and offered a milk-oblation with the *nāgabali* mantra, and having worshipped and offered the consecrated dust (*rajaḥ*) among the *nāgas*, one should cause it to flow away. One should visualize that [the dust] is being led down to the depths of *pātāla* by the *nāgas* with great honor. Having filled the jar into which the dust was led with water, and having offered the consecrated dust among the *nāgas*, one should cause it to flow away. Having brought it back in the same manner, one should sprinkle it with that [water] for the sake of pacification in the maṇḍala house and other locations.

This ritual should be undertaken by yoginīs adorned with cloths offered by patrons; the preceptor or a disciple residing in Oḍḍiyāna should carry it forth, accompanied by the sound of bells, auspicious songs, the music of instruments, and offerings such as parasols, victory banners, and flags, [proceeding] toward great rivers, great lakes, and deep waters.
Sit beside me; having applied butter to a patch of ground, form a maṇḍala with white powder, and in its center draw an eight-petaled lotus.

At the navel, one should worship Vajrasattva and the eight petals with the nagas as before; having offered a milk-porridge *bali* with the *nāga-bali* mantra and performed worship, one should scatter the consecrated colored powders (*rajas*) over the nagas and cast them into the water. One should visualize that the nagas carry [the remains] away to the subterranean realm with great reverence.
Having filled those vases that carried the colored powders with water, one should carry them back to that very spot and scatter them over the mandala house and so forth for the sake of pacification.
Thereafter, that noble-minded man, together with all his kinsmen and clansmen, should cause the maidens to be fed comfortably according to the prescribed rites amidst great festivities;
and he should bestow pure gifts upon the suffering in accordance with his wealth.
For he, being accomplished, respectfully provided food for the Saṅgha along with robes and monetary gifts.

Thereafter, with a noble intention, all the kinsmen together with their attendants should, with great enthusiasm, perform the great marriage ceremony for the young maiden according to the prescribed ritual. Furthermore, the wise should bestow upon her, even though she is suffering, a stainless gift that accords with her prosperity.
He also teaches the Saṅgha with robes and alms-bowls, accompanied by offerings and with reverence.
In this regard, the following is the ritual procedure for the worship of the maiden (kumārī).
Now, this is the ritual for worshipping a maiden:
One established in the prescribed procedure should worship a maiden who has the form of a deity. There, in the consecrated maṇḍala, they should be fed on the ground according to one's capacity.
The young maidens, abiding in the form of goddesses, should be worshipped according to the ritual; having correctly constructed the mandala, one who has the capacity should practice upon that ground.

In whatever maṇḍala there are as many goddesses as there are deities, that many young maidens should be invited on the day prior to the maṇḍala ceremony, following the preliminary rites. Alternatively, one, two, three, or four may be worshipped according to the capacity of the patron (*dānapati*).

In whichever mandala there are as many goddesses as there are, that same number of young maidens should be invited with preliminary offerings such as a maṇḍala and so forth; thereafter, one, two, three, four, or more should be worshipped according to the capacity of the patron.

Then, immediately after the flow of dust, having bathed her with fragrant substances and the like, and having adorned her with red garments and other ornaments, one should respectfully summon her, regarding her as the Blessed Lady herself. Having offered her water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamana*), she should be led into the mandala chamber. Facing eastward, one should place a bundle of *kuśa* grass beneath her seat and have her sit down.

Then, after the colored powders have been removed, one should perform an ablution with fragrant scents and the like, adorn [the deities] with red garments, and with devotion, invite those who have been visualized as the Blessed Lady herself. Having offered water for the feet, water for the face, and so forth, they should be led into the mandala pavilion.
Facing toward the east, one should place bundles of kuśa grass beneath the seat and sit upon them.

Thereafter, the preceptor, having visualized her instantaneously as the Mistress of the Mandala through the transformation of the seed-syllables and emblems within the mandala according to its layout, and having offered the water for honor (*argha*) and other gifts while remaining non-different from the gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*), should bestow vermilion upon her head, a string of beads upon her neck, collyrium-sticks upon her eyes, and ornaments made of red flowers.

Having offered the water for the feet and other offerings to the one who is inseparable from the Jñānasattva, one should also bestow sindhūra upon the head, a string of beads around the neck, collyrium for the eyes applied with a probe, and ornaments of red flowers.
Then, one should worship [the deity] on the forehead, the heart, the hands, and the feet with the four samādhis as they have been obtained,
or with fragrant scents.
Having offered the bali, the mantra-practitioner should then present the food:

solid food (khādya), soft food (bhojya), chewable food (bhakṣya), that which is to be swallowed (prāśya), that which is to be sucked (coṣya), and that which is to be licked (lehyaka); having purified all of this, including the sacrificial porridge (caru), the lamp, and betel-nut (madanaphala), he should offer it.

Having offered the *bali* cake, the mantrin should then present those foods: all kinds of eatables, snacks, and likewise drinks; savory soups, side dishes, and condiments; along with parched grains, lamps, and liquor—all these should be properly prepared and offered.
Endowed with praise and worship, and devoted to the recitation of mantras,
the wise one should worship a young maiden with the desire for the Great Seal (mahāmudrā).
Perfectly endowed with praise and offerings, always diligent in the recitation of mantras, and longing for the great mudrā, the wise one honors young maidens.
And so it is said:
"Likewise,
one should worship with swift effort."
And with intoxicants and even meats, the Vajra goddesses are worshipped by the devoted person who has attained delight in the glorious Vajrayāna.
With contented minds, they become bestowers of boons, for boons are then held within their hands.

If even the *cchaṅ* and meat offerings are presented individually with great diligence and speed by the Vajra goddesses, then those people who perform such offerings with devotion—residing in the glorious Vajrayāna and dwelling in that state of joy—will have their minds perfectly satisfied and will be granted the supreme [attainment]; the supreme [attainments] will certainly abide in their hands.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One in the Śrī-saṃvarodaya.
Thus the Blessed One spoke in the *Śrīsaṃvarodaya* (from the *Herukābhidhāna*).
The signs of the auspicious and inauspicious, however, should be known there in detail;
they have not been stated by me here because of brevity, as I am fearful of prolixity.

O you who fear prolixity! : One should know the characteristics of the virtuous and the non-virtuous in detail; however, they are not stated here because they have been correctly summarized, and because I am afraid of being too wordy.
Then, having offered water for sipping (ācamana), one should smear the hands with fragrant substances;
having given betel nut and the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā), one should cause flowers to be placed in the hand.
Then, having offered water for washing the feet, his hands were anointed with fragrant scents; having offered tooth-cleansing wood and gifts, flowers were presented into his hands.
Then, having received the blessing, one should dedicate the merit;
having performed the dismissal of all [deities], and having paid homage, one should send them back home.
Having received those words of auspiciousness, one should fully dedicate the merit.
Having requested all [the Buddhas] to depart, one should prostrate and request them to return to their own abodes.
Thus, having performed the worship of the young maiden in the mandala,
thereafter—
One should present various excellent flavors of foods—eatables, chewables, drinks, sips, and linctuses—as well as flowers, betel leaves, garments, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then, the Cakra [should be placed] in the house of the Cakra; thereafter, the artisan guild should be satisfied according to one's means.
Afterwards, one should indeed worship and satisfy the village deities, and following that, the deities of the districts.

Following that, one should offer various kinds of food, snacks, and delicacies, along with diverse excellent flavors, drinks, bases, condiments, flowers, tooth-cleansers, garments, and ornaments; and for those who attend to the wheel within the wheel-hall, as well as the assembled artisans, they should be fully satisfied.
Thereafter, one should worship and satisfy the deity who has been consecrated and the local people of that region.

Whatever object has been offered during the rite of consecration— whether in the house, at the door, on the altar, in the sacrificial pit, or upon the pedestal— all of that must indeed be given here to the sovereign preceptor (*ācāryarāja*).
It belongs to no other preceptors, nor does it belong even in the slightest degree to the artisans.
All of that should be applied by the teacher himself, out of his own volition, through the merits of his generosity.

Regarding the houses, doors, pedestals, and the ritual for their consecration, as well as the hearths and the thrones—whatever objects are offered there, all of them belong here to the Master alone; they do not belong to anyone other than the Master, nor does even a fraction of them belong to the artisans.
All of these should be applied with the desire for one's own state of being superior in both generosity and merit.
The patrons, however, having brought the consecrated images and so forth to their own locations with offerings such as music for the purpose of moving them, should perform worship there.
The patrons should take the consecrated images and so forth that are fit for display to their own abodes with offerings such as music and perform worship.
A sacrifice purified by the collections of the scriptures yields auspicious fruit;
and that gift which brings about the fruit of Buddhahood and is beneficial for both [self and others] is easy to give.
When the teacher is established, all happiness arises with certainty for the king, the lord of the place, and the people—those who are proud of the happiness of all sentient beings.

The fruit of the merit thoroughly purified by the oral instructions (*upadeśa*) is that both [the master and the patron] attain the fruit of the Buddhas. Through the gift that brings benefit, the patron is happy; and the master also attains the happiness of bestowing bliss upon all sentient beings through his own consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
The king is certainly and universally virtuous toward the lords of the realm and the people.
Thus concludes the procedure for the dissolution of the maṇḍala.
Thus concludes the ritual for the dissolution of the maṇḍala.
